cards.front: Before you drive, whose seat belts are your job to check, and why do belts matter?
cards.back: Buckle your own seat belt before driving and make sure every passenger uses a belt or child restraint, because belts greatly cut the chance of injury or death in a crash.

cards.front: How should the lap belt and the shoulder belt be worn?
cards.back: Wear the lap belt low and snug across the hips with the shoulder belt across the chest, never under the arm or behind the back, and use both parts of a two-part belt.

cards.front: Why should you wear a seat belt even in a car with air bags?
cards.back: Wear a belt even with air bags, since air bags do not protect you in side or rear impacts or rollovers and will not keep you behind the wheel.

cards.front: What can a deploying air bag do to someone poorly belted, and what distance does NHTSA advise?
cards.back: A deploying air bag can seriously hurt or kill someone who is unbelted or badly belted, and NHTSA advises at least ten inches between the center of the breastbone and the steering wheel hub.

cards.front: Where should children twelve and under ride, and where must a rear-facing infant seat not go?
cards.back: Children twelve and under should always ride properly restrained in a back seat, and a rear-facing infant seat must never go in front of an active passenger air bag.

cards.front: Who does the general Missouri seat belt law require to wear a fastened belt?
cards.back: Missouri law requires the driver and front seat passengers of every passenger vehicle to wear a properly adjusted, fastened seat belt.

cards.front: Who must be properly restrained when an intermediate license holder is driving?
cards.back: When an intermediate license holder is driving, every passenger in the vehicle must be properly restrained.

cards.front: How does the reach of the belt law change when an intermediate license holder drives?
cards.back: The general belt law covers the driver and front seat riders, but with an intermediate license holder at the wheel the duty extends to every passenger.

cards.front: When must a child under four ride in a suitable child restraint system?
cards.back: A child under four years old must ride in a suitable child restraint system no matter how much the child weighs.

cards.front: When must a child weighing under forty pounds ride in a suitable child restraint system?
cards.back: A child weighing under forty pounds must ride in a suitable child restraint system no matter how old the child is.

cards.front: How do the age tier and the weight tier for the youngest children relate to each other?
cards.back: The two youngest restraint tiers work independently: under four years needs a child restraint at any weight, and under forty pounds needs one at any age.

cards.front: Which child must ride in a child restraint system or a booster seat?
cards.back: A child aged four to under eight who weighs from forty to under eighty pounds and is shorter than four feet nine inches must ride in a child restraint system or booster seat.

cards.front: Which child may use a vehicle safety belt or a suitable booster seat?
cards.back: A child who is at least eight, at least eighty pounds, or taller than four feet nine inches must use a vehicle safety belt or a suitable booster seat.

cards.front: How do the conditions for the booster tier differ from those for the safety belt tier?
cards.back: The booster tier needs all three conditions at once, while the safety belt tier is reached by meeting any one of eight years, eighty pounds or more than four feet nine inches.

cards.front: Which vehicles does the child restraint law cover?
cards.back: The child restraint law covers transport in any motor vehicle other than a school bus or a public carrier for hire.

cards.front: How should a defensive driver move their eyes, and why watch oncoming traffic?
cards.back: Defensive drivers keep their eyes moving ahead, to the sides and behind through the mirrors every few seconds, and watch oncoming traffic, since distracted drivers crossing the center line cause many head-on crashes.

cards.front: What should you expect of other drivers, and what must you not do even when someone fails to yield?
cards.back: Expect other drivers to make mistakes, such as not stopping at a stop sign, plan how you would react, and never cause a crash on purpose even when someone fails to yield.

cards.front: Should you rely on signals or signs to keep others from crossing your path at intersections?
cards.back: Do not count on signals or signs to stop others from crossing your path; look left and right at intersections even when cross traffic faces a red light or stop sign.

cards.front: How far ahead should you look while steering, and why?
cards.back: Look well down the road, not just right in front of the hood, to spot places you will need to steer or slow before you reach them.

cards.front: What does good driving posture look like?
cards.back: Good posture means sitting straight and relaxed against the seat, close enough to reach the pedals but with elbows still in front of you, both feet near the controls and both hands on the wheel.

cards.front: Where should your left and right hands hold the steering wheel?
cards.back: Hold the wheel with your left hand between the seven and nine o'clock positions and your right hand between three and five o'clock.

cards.front: What do the recommended hand positions on the wheel let you do?
cards.back: The seven-to-nine and three-to-five hand positions are comfortable and let you make most turns without letting go of the wheel.

cards.front: How should you steer around corners and straighten out after a turn?
cards.back: Steer around corners with the hand-over-hand method rather than palming the wheel with one hand, and straighten the wheel by hand after the turn.

cards.front: What happens if you turn the ignition key to the lock position while moving?
cards.back: Never turn the ignition key to the lock position while the vehicle is moving, because the steering wheel will lock when you turn it and you will lose control.

cards.front: What causes the very common rear-end crash?
cards.back: Rear-end crashes are very common and are caused by drivers following so closely that they cannot stop when the car ahead stops suddenly.

cards.front: How does the three second rule tell you that you are following too closely?
cards.back: Under the three second rule, start counting when the car ahead passes a fixed object, and if you reach the object before you count to three, you are too close.

cards.front: How can you help the driver behind you keep a safe gap?
cards.back: Help the driver behind keep a safe gap by holding a steady speed and signaling early before you slow down.

cards.front: What should you do when a tailgater follows you?
cards.back: If a tailgater follows you and there is a right lane, move into it; if not, wait for clear road and slow down gradually, never braking suddenly.

cards.front: What should you do if you are slowing other drivers down?
cards.back: If you are slowing others down, pull aside when safe to let them pass, using turnouts on some two-lane roads; other two-lane roads may offer passing lanes.

cards.front: What should you do if traffic is behind you when you want to parallel park?
cards.back: If traffic is behind you when you want to parallel park, signal, pull up beside the space and wait for the traffic to pass before you back in.

cards.front: Where should you pick up or drop off passengers?
cards.back: Pick a safe spot out of traffic to pick up or drop off passengers.

cards.front: How should you place your car among other vehicles on multi-lane roads and within your lane?
cards.back: Avoid driving alongside other vehicles on multi-lane roads, keep away from oncoming traffic by not crowding the center line, and generally stay in the middle of your lane.

cards.front: Why should you keep a wider gap from parked cars?
cards.back: Keep a wider gap from parked cars, because someone may step out of or between them, or one may pull out.

cards.front: What should you do when traffic is merging onto a multi-lane road and the lane beside you is empty?
cards.back: When traffic is merging onto a multi-lane road and the lane beside you is empty, move over a lane to make room.

cards.front: How should you handle pedestrians, cyclists and more than one hazard?
cards.back: Give pedestrians and cyclists, especially children, extra room, and take hazards one at a time, for example letting an oncoming car pass before you overtake a cyclist.
cards.memory_hook: extra room, one at a time

cards.front: What two distances make up stopping distance, and what increases it?
cards.back: Stopping distance is reaction distance plus braking distance, and speed, fatigue or poor brakes all increase it.

cards.front: What is reaction distance, and what reaction time does the guide's chart assume?
cards.back: Reaction distance is how far you travel between seeing a danger and braking, and the guide's chart assumes a reaction time of one point five seconds.

cards.front: What is braking distance, and what conditions does the chart assume?
cards.back: Braking distance is how far you travel from applying the brakes to a full stop, and the chart assumes good brakes, tires, weather and road.

cards.front: Which part of stopping distance comes before you touch the brake, and which comes after?
cards.back: Reaction distance is covered before you touch the brake, while braking distance is covered after; together they make stopping distance.

cards.front: What do other drivers expect you to keep doing, and why warn them before you change direction or slow down?
cards.back: Other drivers expect you to keep doing what you are doing, so warn them before you change direction or slow down to give them time to react.

cards.front: When should you use your turn signal?
cards.back: Signal before changing lanes, turning, merging or parking, and do it every time you change direction even if no one seems to be around.

cards.front: How far ahead should you signal, and when should you wait to signal?
cards.back: Signal at least one hundred feet ahead, but if streets, driveways or entrances lie between you and your turn, wait until you pass them before signaling.

cards.front: What is the exception to signaling at least one hundred feet before a turn?
cards.back: The signaling rule of at least one hundred feet has an exception: hold the signal until you pass any streets, driveways or entrances before your turn, or a vehicle about to enter between you and the turn.

cards.front: What should you check after a turn or lane change, and why?
cards.back: After a turn or lane change make sure the signal has shut off, because a signal left blinking can make others think you will turn again.

cards.front: What should you do if your turn signal has not clicked off after a small turn?
cards.back: A turn signal may not cancel itself after a small turn, so switch it off by hand if it has not clicked off.

decks.module: Horn, slow driving and carbon monoxide
decks.domain: Missouri everyday safe driving: seat belts and child restraints, defensive driving, posture and steering, following distance, space cushions, stopping distance, signaling, horn use, slow driving, carbon monoxide, deer crashes, tires and traffic stops

cards.front: What is the only reason to sound your horn?
cards.back: The only reason to sound your horn is to warn other drivers, and needless honking can distract others and cause a crash.

cards.front: Is the horn for showing anger or frustration?
cards.back: The horn is never for showing anger or frustration.

cards.front: Is it legal to drive below a posted minimum speed?
cards.back: Driving below a posted minimum speed in normal conditions is illegal, though bad weather, heavy traffic or a bad road can justify going slower.

cards.front: With no posted minimum, can slow driving still be illegal, and what should you do if vehicles line up behind you?
cards.back: Even with no posted minimum, it is illegal to drive so slowly that you block traffic, and if vehicles line up behind you, pull over and let them pass.

cards.front: What can excuse going below a posted minimum, and when is slow driving illegal with no minimum posted?
cards.back: Going below a posted minimum is excused only by bad weather, heavy traffic or a bad road, while blocking traffic by slow driving is illegal even with no minimum posted.

cards.front: How do you avoid carbon monoxide when the car is parked or in a garage?
cards.back: Avoid carbon monoxide by never running the engine in a garage or in a parked car with the windows shut, including running the heater or air conditioner.

cards.front: How do you guard against carbon monoxide while you are driving?
cards.back: Carbon monoxide from the engine is a deadly gas, so close the vents when following closely behind another vehicle and never drive with a broken muffler or exhaust.

cards.front: What should you expect after seeing one deer crossing or a struck deer by the road?
cards.back: Deer rarely travel alone, so if you see one crossing or a struck deer by the road, expect more nearby, especially near fields, streams and gardens.

cards.front: When do most deer crashes happen, by month and by time of day?
cards.back: Most deer crashes happen in January, May and October through December, and the riskiest times are sunset to midnight and around sunrise.

cards.front: Where should you take extra care for deer, and how can belts help if a deer crash happens?
cards.back: Take extra care where deer crossing signs are posted, and keep everyone belted and children in car seats to reduce injury if a deer crash happens.

cards.front: When should you use high beams to spot deer, and how do they help?
cards.back: At night with no oncoming traffic, use high beams, which light up the eyes of deer near the road and give you more time to react.

cards.front: If hitting a deer cannot be avoided, should you swerve?
cards.back: If hitting a deer cannot be avoided, do not swerve, because leaving the road or crossing into oncoming traffic raises the risk of injury.

cards.front: What should you check before slowing hard for a deer, and why?
cards.back: Before slowing hard for a deer, make sure no one is behind you; heavy braking can dip the front end so the deer's body comes through into the passenger area.

cards.front: What should you do after a deer crash?
cards.back: After a deer crash, report it to local law enforcement, get a police report if your insurer needs one, and tell a local Department of Conservation agent where it happened.

cards.front: Where do you find the right tire pressure, and how do you set it?
cards.back: Read the right tire pressure in the owner's manual or on the driver's door jamb, check it with a gauge, and add or release air until it matches.

cards.front: How often should you check your tires for wear and damage?
cards.back: Check tires for wear and damage once a month or before a long trip.

cards.front: What should you do when emergency lights appear behind you?
cards.back: When emergency lights appear behind you, stay calm, signal, and pull off or to the side as soon as it is safe.

cards.front: What should you do once an officer has stopped you?
cards.back: Once stopped, turn off the engine and radio, stay inside unless told to get out, keep your hands on the wheel, and do not use phones or search for documents until the officer asks.

cards.front: What should you ask passengers to do at a traffic stop?
cards.back: Ask passengers at a traffic stop to stay calm, remain in the vehicle and keep their hands where the officer can see them.

cards.front: What should you do at night once you stop for an officer, and why?
cards.back: At night an officer may shine a spotlight on your car, so turn on the interior lights once you stop to help the officer see inside.

cards.front: When should you tell the officer about a weapon in the vehicle?
cards.back: If there is a weapon in the vehicle, tell the officer when the officer first makes contact.

cards.front: What should you do if your documents are out of reach, and what can you expect of an officer out of uniform?
cards.back: Tell the officer where your documents are before reaching for them if they are out of reach, and expect an officer out of uniform to show credentials, which you may also request.

cards.front: If an officer asks you to step out of the vehicle, what should you do?
cards.back: If asked to step out of the vehicle, stay well away from traffic and keep your hands visible.

cards.front: Does signing a traffic ticket admit guilt, and where should you contest it?
cards.back: Signing a traffic ticket is not an admission of guilt, but refusing to sign it may lead to arrest; contest it in court rather than arguing at the roadside.

cards.front: What should you do if you think an officer acted improperly?
cards.back: If you think an officer acted improperly, record what happened and report it promptly to that officer's agency, whose name and the officer's name appear on the ticket or can be requested.

cards.front: What constitutional rights do you keep during a traffic stop?
cards.back: During a traffic stop you keep constitutional rights, including freedom from unreasonable search and seizure, the right to remain silent and the right to an attorney.

recap_hooks.text: Buckle yourself and see that every rider has a belt or child restraint, lap belt low on the hips and shoulder belt across the chest.
Air bags work with belts, not instead of them, so sit well back from the wheel and keep kids twelve and under in back.
Missouri law belts the driver and front seat riders, and every passenger when an intermediate license holder drives.
Under four years or under forty pounds, either one alone, means a child restraint system.
The booster tier needs age, weight and height all at once; the belt tier opens with any one of eight years, eighty pounds or more than four feet nine inches.
The law reaches every motor vehicle except a school bus or a public carrier for hire.
Keep your eyes moving, expect others to slip up, and look both ways even when cross traffic has a red light.
Sit straight with elbows in front, hands at seven-to-nine and three-to-five, and steer hand-over-hand.
The key never goes to lock while the car is moving.
Count three seconds behind the car ahead, and give the driver behind a steady speed and an early signal.
A tailgater gets the right lane or a gradual slowdown, and you pull aside when you are the one holding others up.
Keep room beside you: skip side-by-side driving, widen the gap from parked cars, make room for mergers and give walkers and cyclists extra space.
Stopping distance is the ground you cover reacting plus the ground you cover braking.
Warn others by signaling every direction change at least one hundred feet out, but wait until you pass side streets and driveways before the turn.
After the turn, check that the signal is off and cancel it by hand if needed.

recaps.module: Horn, slow driving and carbon monoxide

recap_hooks.text: The horn warns; it is not for anger.
Below the posted minimum is legal only in bad weather, heavy traffic or on a bad road, and blocking traffic is illegal even with no minimum.
Never run the engine in a garage or a shut-up parked car, and close the vents when following closely.
One deer means more nearby, especially from sunset to midnight and around sunrise, so use high beams when no one is coming.
If a deer hit cannot be avoided, do not swerve, check behind before hard braking, and report the crash afterward.
Set tire pressure from the manual or door jamb, check tires monthly, and use the penny test on the tread.
Lights behind you mean calm, signal and pull over, then engine and radio off and hands on the wheel.
Mention a weapon at first contact, say where your documents are before reaching, and keep your hands visible outside the car.
Signing a ticket admits nothing, you keep your rights, and disputes go to court or to the officer's agency.
